podcast.title: Pioneering Vinyl Release (1931)
podcast.body: RCA, described as one of the most important record labels globally for 50 to 60 years, released the first polyvinyl chloride disc in 1931, which is the material used for modern vinyl records. "la que fue casi la disco gráfica más importante del mundo durante 50 a 60 años, que fue la RCA sacó el primer disco de cloruro de polivinilo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ESPECIAL FORMATOS: Historia del Vinilo.

podcast.title: Reaction to Columbia's LP Unveiling (1948)
podcast.body: Columbia Records invited RCA executives to a private demonstration of their new LP technology in April 1948, two months before the public press conference. RCA "freaked out" upon realizing they had been severely "scooped" by technology they once possessed but had allowed to slip away due to a "dumb clerical error" (referring to their expired patents). Despite being offered a license for the technology, RCA refused. "Columbia invited RCA executives into their boardroom in April 1948, some two months before that big press conference, to demonstrate their new technology. RCA freaked out because they knew that they'd been scooped and scooped badly, and with technology that they once possessed. But let slip away due to some dumb clerical error. They offered to license the technology to RCA, but they said, no, no thanks."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 1

podcast.title: Color-Coded Vinyl Records (1949)
podcast.body: Upon the launch of the 7-inch single, RCA introduced a system of color-coding records by genre. Country music was pressed on green vinyl, serious classical on red, popular classical on midnight blue, children's records on yellow, international songs on sky blue, Rhythm and Blues on "saris" (not red), and everyday pop records on black vinyl. While a "nice idea," this system did not last very long. "RCA had come up with a system of color coding records by genre. Country was green. Serious classical was red. Popular classical was midnight blue. Yellow was reserved for children's records. International songs were sky blue. Rhythm and blues was saris. Not red, saris. And your everyday pop records were on block vinyl. It was a nice idea, but it didn't last very long."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 1

podcast.title: Introduction of 7-inch Single (1949)
podcast.body: In March 1949, RCA introduced the 7-inch single, which was initially designed to be played exclusively on special turntables manufactured by RCA. These record players were relatively small, described as being the size of a squat blender, offering a degree of portability, though they still required an electrical outlet. The prominent large hole in the center was a distinctive design feature of these records. `"When RCA introduced the 7-inch single in March of 1949, the original idea was to make them playable only on special turn tables made by RCA."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Introduction of the 45 RPM Single (1949)
podcast.body: RCA Records unveiled the 7-inch, 45 RPM single in March 1949, serving as its direct response to Columbia Records' introduction of the LP. "Texarkana Baby" by Eddie Arnold was among the initial 45s released. "RCA Records responded to Columbia's LP with the 7 inch 45 RPM single."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts

podcast.title: Madam X Project and 7-inch Single Development (1949)
podcast.body: After Columbia's LP announcement, RCA initiated project "Madam X" to develop its own vinyl record format to protect its market dominance. Engineers revisited 1930s archives and found notes from 1901 indicating experiments with a single-song format. As a consumer electronics company, RCA also planned to manufacture dedicated record players for their new records. This led to the introduction of the 7-inch single in February 1949. "Meanwhile, RCA knew that they had to do something. Otherwise, their market dominance in both North America and Europe would be in jeopardy. The one thing they did realize is that vinyl was a much better raw material for records than shellac, so they drew up plans for their own version of the vinyl record. They called the project Madam X."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 1

podcast.title: Elvis Presley's Signing Bonus (1955)
podcast.body: As part of the deal to acquire Elvis Presley's contract from Sun Records in 1955, RCA paid Elvis a $5,000 signing bonus, a significant portion of which was directed into Tom Parker's pocket. "to pay Elvis a $5,000 signing bonus, of which, of course, a big chunk went directly into Tom Parker's pocket."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 33: "Mystery Train", by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Early Recognition of Million-Selling Singles (1956)
podcast.body: In 1956, RCA Records presented Elvis Presley with a gold record for selling one million copies of his single "Don't Be Cruel." This act by a record label preceded the formalization of sales awards by the RIAA. "In 1956, RCA presented one to Elvis Presley for selling one million copies of his single Don't Be Cruel."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts

podcast.title: Reissue of Sun Single (1956)
podcast.body: The very first action RCA Records took after signing Elvis Presley was to reissue his last Sun single, "I Forgot to Remember to Forget," which then hit number one on the country charts with their backing. "The first thing RCA did was to reissue his last Sun single. I forgot to remember to forget."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 38: "Heartbreak Hotel" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Signed Janice Martin at 15 (March 1956)
podcast.body: RCA Records, one of the biggest labels, signed Janice Martin in March 1956 when she was just 15 years old, following A&R man Steve Sholes' lead after he had signed Elvis Presley. "in March 1956, aged just 15, Janice Martin was signed to RCA Records, one of the biggest labels in the country."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: World's Largest Record Company (1956)
podcast.body: In 1956, RCA was recognized as the largest record company in the world when Elvis Presley signed with them, providing him with unparalleled promotional resources. "la RCA que era la discográfica más grande del mundo de aquellas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Elvis Presley - El día que nació el mito

podcast.title: Pushed for Abortion and Dropped Janice Martin (1957)
podcast.body: Upon learning of Janice Martin's pregnancy in 1957, RCA was furious, believing it incompatible with her "nation's sweetheart" image. They attempted to persuade her to get an abortion (which was illegal), and when she refused, they dropped her from the label. "They tried to persuade her to get an abortion, although that was still illegal in the US at the time. She refused, and the label dropped her."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: RCA's "How to Listen to New Dimensions in Sound" (1957)
podcast.body: In 1957, RCA produced a short film titled "How to Listen to New Dimensions in Sound" to educate and promote stereo sound to consumers. This film discussed the appreciation of music at home and the pursuit of "perfect fidelity." "RCA released a short film entitled How to Listen to New Dimensions in Sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of Stereo: Part 1

podcast.title: Colonel Parker's Leverage Against RCA (1958)
podcast.body: Colonel Parker intentionally orchestrated Elvis's full military service to limit the creation of a large backlog of recordings for RCA. His strategic goal was to make RCA keenly aware of their dependence on "the Colonel" during Elvis's two-year absence from professional recording. "If he didn't give RCA much of a backlog to release while he was away, RCA would realise how much they needed the Colonel."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Leiber and Stoller's Employment (c. 1958)
podcast.body: At the time they were writing for Elvis, Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller were employed as staff songwriters for RCA. Despite Colonel Parker's desire to remove them, he allowed them to continue working because they were consistently generating hit songs for the label. "They were currently working for RCA, so while that was the case, he would put them to use, but they were loose cannons."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Stockpile Strategy (1958-1960)
podcast.body: RCA successfully implemented a plan by Colonel Parker to record a "tiny stockpile of recordings" in 1958, allowing them to issue singles like "My Ring Around Your Neck," "Hard Headed Woman," and "A Big Hunk O' Love" over the two years Elvis Presley was in the army, keeping him in the spotlight despite no new material. "He'd recorded and off in 1958, for R.C.E. to have a tiny stockpile of recordings they could issue as singles over the intervening two years."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 82: "Are You Lonesome Tonight?" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Advance Single Orders (1960)
podcast.body: For Elvis Presley's first post-army single, "Stuck On You," RCA printed an astounding 1.4 million copies "just to fulfill the advanced orders" within 72 hours of the single's release. This was done even before the specific songs were known, leading to generic sleeve printing. "By that time, RCA had printed up 1.4 million copies of the single, just to fulfill the advanced orders."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 82: "Are You Lonesome Tonight?" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Car Turntables (1960-1961)
podcast.body: RCA entered the market for in-car record players in 1960 and 1961, offering units that played standard 45 RPM records. However, a significant drawback was that the stylus had to press very heavily on the record to prevent skipping on bumpy roads, which caused the records to wear out quickly. `"then RCA got into the act in 1960 and 1961. These ones played standard 45 RPM records, but because the stylists had to press so heavily on the record to keep from skipping on bumpy roads, records wore out really fast."`

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Cautious Approach with Charlie Pride (1965)
podcast.body: RCA, under legendary producer Chet Atkins, offered Charlie Pride a recording contract in 1965. However, the label adopted a very cautious approach initially, not using Pride's photo on promotional materials and testing audience reactions in different towns before scheduling further shows, due to concerns about his race. "Still, RCA, they took a very cautious approach with Pride at first."

podcast.title: Exclusivity for Black Country Artists (1967-1991)
podcast.body: RCA was the only major record label to sign an African-American country singer between 1967 and 1991, with Charlie Pride being that artist. This highlights the lack of diversity and representation for black artists within major country music labels for nearly a quarter-century. "he was the only African-American country singer that was signed to a major record label between 1967 and 1991. That was RCA."

podcast.title: Quad-8 Tapes (1970)
podcast.body: In 1970, RCA introduced "Quad-8" quadraphonic 8-track tapes. These tapes were ultimately unsuccessful due to their poor quality and were withdrawn from the market by 1976. "In 1970, RCA introduced a quad-8-track tape they called the Quad-8. But they weren't very good and disappeared from the marketplace by 1976."

podcast.title: Response to David Bowie's Album Cover Controversy (1971)
podcast.body: RCA Records had to intervene when *The Man Who Sold the World* album, featuring David Bowie in a dress on its original cover, was refused by many American record stores in 1971. To address this sales impediment, the label supplied an alternative cover. "And many record stores refused to stock the album until RCA records supplied them with a different cover."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1

podcast.title: Invention of the Flex Disc (1972)
podcast.body: RCA invented the "Flex disc" in 1972, a significant development that standardized vinyl production and became the common format used throughout the 1970s, 1980s, 1990s, and almost up to the present day. "cuando también la RCA, inventa el disco flex, el disco flex es el vinilo estándar que se usó durante todos los 70 a 80 a 90 y hasta casi hoy en día."

podcast.title: John Denver's Greatest Hits Release (1973)
podcast.body: RCA, John Denver's label, issued the compilation 'John Denver's Greatest Hits' in late 1973, for which he re-recorded several tracks. "his label, RCA, had issued a compilation. My beloved John Denver's greatest hits."

podcast.title: Strategic Re-promotion of David Bowie's Catalog (1973-1974)
podcast.body: As David Bowie broke on the album chart in 1972 with LPs like "Hunky Dory" and "Ziggy Stardust," RCA Records, his American label, strategically re-promoted his 1969 album (under the title "Space Oddity") and re-issued singles like "Space Oddity" and "Changes" in the early 1970s, crucial actions that solidified Bowie's career in America. "RCA Records, Bowie's American label, decided to re-promote his 1969 album, under the title Space Audity, with new post-Ziggy Stardust imagery and even a new video of Bowie miming the song in glam makeup."

podcast.title: Diamond Dogs Censorship (1974)
podcast.body: RCA, David Bowie's record label, airbrushed out the "prominent set of dog junk" from the original 1974 "Diamond Dogs" album cover, which depicted Bowie as half-man, half-dog, because the artwork was considered too outrageous. "An unknown number of copies were sold before RCA Bowie's label put an end to that by airbrushing out the dog junk."

srcs.episode: Valuable Vinyl

podcast.title: Remix and Single Release for "Rock the Boat" (1974)
podcast.body: RCA executives, upon learning of "Rock the Boat's" popularity in New York clubs, released a remixed dance version as a single in 1974, which then topped the Billboard Hot 100. "When RCA executives got wind of this in 1974, they released a remixed dance version and they released Rock The Boat as a single and it took off."

podcast.title: Contract Dispute with Lou Reed (1975)
podcast.body: In 1975, RCA Records was in a contract dispute with Lou Reed, who wished to terminate his agreement. The label insisted he fulfill his contractual obligation of delivering a certain number of albums. "He wanted out of his contract, but RCA was adamant. He had to provide them with the required number of albums as stipulated in his contract."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 3: Industrial

podcast.title: Lou Reed's "Metal Machine Music" Release (1975)
podcast.body: RCA released Lou Reed's experimental double album "Metal Machine Music" in the summer of 1975, not out of artistic support, but as a retaliatory move against Reed who was trying to get out of his contract. Reed was contractually obligated to deliver more albums and delivered this avant-garde work of noise and feedback, which RCA, in an "in-your-face" response, put out to the public. "RCA said, screw you and released it as an in-your-face move back at Lou."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Distortion and Feedback

podcast.title: Reluctance to Release Low (1976)
podcast.body: RCA initially refused to release David Bowie's album "Low" because they did not consider it a guaranteed success, despite Bowie's prior consistent chart performance. They suggested he rework the album with more commercially viable hits.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.title: Promotion of Heroes (1977)
podcast.body: Following the unexpected success of "Low," RCA put significant commercial pressure and heavily invested in advertising and press for David Bowie's "Heroes." They used the iconic slogan: "There's Old Wave, there's New Wave, and there's David Bowie," to promote him as an innovator of fresh, new music.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.title: Failed Collaboration with Joy Division (1978)
podcast.body: RCA signed Joy Division in 1978, providing a substantial budget and good producers. However, the label's attempt to create a "prefabricated product" aligning with the punk trend clashed with the band's desire for new sounds, leading to a failed collaboration and Joy Division abandoning the label. "Durante 1978 los JVS empiezan a trabajar en los estudios de la RCA con bastante presupuesto y además con bastantes buenos productores y acaba siendo un fracaso."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 1. Inicios en la escena post-punk

podcast.title: Hunting for Punk-like Bands (1978)
podcast.body: In 1978, RCA and other record labels were aggressively seeking out bands that emulated the Sex Pistols' punk sound or played verbally aggressive music, viewing it as a highly profitable market. "tanto la RCA, pues como muchas otras discográficas estaban comentivamente a la caza de cualquier grupo que pudiesen echar un poco más mercado que diez, un poco ese aire pan de los expuestos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 1. Inicios en la escena post-punk

podcast.title: Poor Distribution of "Black Tie White Noise" (1993)
podcast.body: David Bowie's 1993 album "Black Tie White Noise" was released on a "small subsidiary of RCA Records" and suffered from poor distribution and promotion. This logistical failure contributed significantly to the album barely scraping the top 40 and becoming his shortest-lived album on the Billboard 200. "Unfortunately, Black Tie White Noise was released on a small subsidiary of RCA Records and was poorly distributed and promoted."

podcast.title: "Next Elvis" Strategy and Production Flaws
podcast.body: RCA Records signed Roy Orbison, envisioning him as "the next Elvis," and used many of the same session musicians from Elvis's big hits. However, the label's producers failed to understand Orbison's unique voice and style, pushing him to sing pop-country ballads not of his choosing, leading to singles performing worse than his Sun records. "Roy bought a Cadillac, moved to Nashville, and quickly signed with RCA records, who saw in him the potential to be the next Elvis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "Space Oddity" Demo and Release
podcast.body: David Bowie demoed "Space Oddity" for executives at RCA Records after the song had been rejected multiple times. RCA ultimately released the song, which became Bowie's first hit. "But then he had a chance to demo it for some people at RCA Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1

podcast.title: Acquisition of Elvis Presley's Contract
podcast.body: RCA's acquisition of Elvis Presley's contract from Sun Records involved a substantial payment, which provided critical financial security to Sam Phillips's label. Steve Sholes, an RCA executive, later expressed concern to Sam Phillips about "backed the wrong horse" when Carl Perkins's "Blue Suede Shoes" began competing directly with Elvis's "Heartbreak Hotel" on the charts. "With the amount of money that RCA had paid for Elvis's contract, Sun Records was, for the first time, on a completely secure footing"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Alleged Chart Interference for Andy Gibb
podcast.body: RCA, Andy Gibb's record label, is legendarily accused of threatening Billboard or Casey Kasem to ensure Andy Gibb's "Shadow Dancing" remained at number one, thereby preventing Gerry Rafferty's "Baker Street" from reaching the top spot and contributing to its status as a famous all-time number 2 hit. "RCA, Andy Gibb's record label allegedly threatened to not let him take part in some sort of billboard show If shadow dancing was not still number 1"

podcast.title: Attempt to Entice Elvis Presley
podcast.body: RCA, Elvis Presley's record label, converted a room at Graceland (the "Jungle Room") into a recording studio in October 1976. This was an attempt to entice Elvis to record new material, as he had become increasingly reclusive and difficult to motivate for studio sessions during the mid to late 1970s. "And it was converted into a recording studio because RCA, his record label at that time, hoped that it would entice Elvis to actually record something."

podcast.title: Chet Atkins' Self-Blame
podcast.body: Chet Atkins, involved in Orbison's RCA recordings, later expressed regret and self-blame for not recognizing Orbison's true potential. He characterized the records as "typical Nashville at that time" and admitted they failed to "reach out and try to do something different" or see "the greatness in him and the quality of his voice." "Chet Atkins, like Sam Phillips, just didn't get Roy Orbison. He would later say, we did some pretty good records, but they were typical Nashville at that time, and we didn't reach out and try to do something different. I blame myself for that. I should have seen the greatness in him and the quality of his voice."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Closure of Groove Records
podcast.body: Following the breakthrough success of Mickey & Sylvia's "Love Is Strange" on Groove Records, RCA made the decision to close the subsidiary label. The artists and producer were then moved to another RCA subsidiary, Vic Records. "But after groove records that had this breakthrough big hit, RCA decided to close the label down and move the acts on the label and their producer Valence to another subsidiary. Vic."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 49: "Love is Strange" by Mickey and Sylvia

podcast.title: Compromise on Music Video
podcast.body: RCA secured a deal with The Strokes, largely because they were accommodating of the band's desire to make a music video. This flexibility played a role in RCA winning the bidding war for their US distribution rights. "They also landed a deal with RCA, largely because they were okay with The Stroke Desire to make a music video."

podcast.title: Conferrer of the First Gold Record
podcast.body: RCA was the record label that awarded the very first documented gold record in February 1942 to Glenn Miller for his single "Chattanooga Choo Choo," commemorating its sale of 1.2 million units.

podcast.title: Country Department Affiliation
podcast.body: Janice Martin was signed by RCA's country department, which led to her being placed on concert bills with other RCA country artists like Hank Snow, despite her rock and roll style being incompatible. "she had come up through the country music scene and had been signed by RCA's country department."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Creation of "Fake Indie Labels"
podcast.body: RCA, like other major labels, created wholly owned subsidiaries like Groove Records (established 1953) as "fake indie labels." This strategy was employed to sell to R&B customers and shops who preferred independent labels and were uninterested in the major labels' mainstream offerings like Doris Day or Frank Sinatra. "And so, those labels set up their own mini-divisions to sell to those shops. They had different labels because the shops wouldn't buy from the majors, but they were wholly owned subsidiaries. Fake indie labels. And Groove was one of them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: David Bowie Deal (Early 1970s)
podcast.body: RCA Records secured a new deal with David Bowie in the early 1970s, approximately 18 months after Tony DeFries signed on as Bowie's manager. This deal was pivotal in launching Bowie as an international star.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock

podcast.title: David Bowie's Dissatisfaction and Departure (Early 1980s)
podcast.body: David Bowie was unhappy with RCA Records, which led to the longest gap in his career between studio albums as he angled to get out of his contract, ultimately moving to EMI Records for his "Let's Dance" album in 1983. This dissatisfaction marked a turning point in his career and label affiliations. "He was unhappy with his label, RCA Records, angling to get out of the contract and determined to try new things."

podcast.title: David Bowie's Early Career Label
podcast.body: David Bowie was with RCA Records during the period when he entered into a problematic management arrangement with Tony DeFrees, and he remained with them even after parting ways with DeFrees in 1975. "He was still with RCA records, but he had left DeFrees behind in 1975."

srcs.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 2

podcast.title: Development of the Spider Adapter
podcast.body: RCA developed the "spider" adapter, a three-armed, usually yellow or red plastic insert, to allow 45s to be played on turntables with standard LP-sized spindles. These spiders had "drive dots" that interlocked when records were stacked, preventing slippage. "This was RCA's idea. Spiders looked like a three-armed galaxy, usually yellow or red, and each was made of plastic."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 3

podcast.title: Dropping and Re-signing Pure Prairie League
podcast.body: RCA initially dropped Pure Prairie League after the release of their 1972 album "Bustin' Out," largely due to co-founder Craig Fuller's legal issues as a conscientious objector. However, the label later re-signed the band and re-released the song "Amy" as a single after it gained significant popularity on college, country, and Top 40 radio stations. "but then RCA dropped them no doubt do at least in part to these legal problems that Craig Fuller had brought upon himself."

podcast.title: Dynaflex Recording Promotion
podcast.body: RCA promoted David Bowie's 1971 album "The Man Who Sold the World" as a "Dynaflex recording," a new development in record manufacturing. This technology aimed to provide a smoother, quieter surface and improved sound quality, while also making records lighter to eliminate warpage and turntable slippage. "RCA was very proud to mention that this album was a dino-flex recording, a new development and record manufacturing that provides a smoother quieter surface and improves sound quality to reproduce a musical sound."

podcast.title: Early Large Label
podcast.body: RCA is mentioned as one of the historically larger record labels from an era when the industry had many independent players before market consolidation. "They were some that were bigger than others like Deca and London and RCA and EMI, but there were literally thousands of small labels that did their own thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Early Vinyl Experimentation and Patent Lapse (1930s)
podcast.body: In 1931, RCA experimented with polyvinyl chloride as a superior replacement for the materials used in 78 RPM records. They even produced 12-inch vinyl records, ready for public sale, but the Great Depression prevented their release. Consequently, RCA allowed many of their crucial patents related to this vinyl technology to expire, a decision later regarded as "dumb" as Columbia Records would later use similar principles for the LP. "Then in 1931, RCA was experimenting with vinyl as a replacement for the crappy materials that went into making 78s. RCA even started making vinyl records that were 12 inches in diameter, and were ready to sell them to the general public. But it was the depression. And no one was in the mood for introducing a new format into what seemed at the time to be a dying industry... So not only did RCA give up, but they also led a bunch of their patents expire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 1

podcast.title: Esquivel's Experimental Recording Hub
podcast.body: El edificio de la RCA en Hollywood fue el escenario de las revolucionarias técnicas de grabación de Juan García Esquivel. Para su álbum "Latin-esque" de 1962, Esquivel colocó dos orquestas en estudios separados dentro del edificio (estudio 1 y estudio 2), logrando una separación estéreo extrema y efectos sonoros únicos mediante un sistema de sincronización con auriculares y comunicación telefónica. "dentro del edificio de la RCA en Hollywood, un en el estudio 1 y la otra en el estudio 2."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Así sonaba el pop de la era atómica

podcast.title: Establishment of Nashville Studio
podcast.body: Ethel Gabriel worked with RCA to establish their renowned studio in Nashville, playing a key role in developing the label's presence in a vital music hub. Her involvement extended beyond production into infrastructure development and the label's strategic growth. "She worked with RCA to establish their famous studio as a Nashville."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Unsung Heroines

podcast.title: Extensive Promotion of Elvis Presley
podcast.body: Upon signing Elvis Presley in 1956, RCA immediately began an aggressive promotional campaign, leveraging its extensive resources to secure large concerts, television promotion, magazine features, and widespread media coverage for the artist. "la RCA nada más cogera el BISPRESLEI empieza a promocionarlo con los recursos que tenía."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Elvis Presley - El día que nació el mito

podcast.title: Failed Contract with Joy Division
podcast.body: Joy Division had a failed recording contract with RCA prior to recording *Unknown Pleasures*. During this period, they had already made a recording, developing a blend of punk and new wave. This experience gave them a clear artistic vision when they entered the studio for their debut album. "habían tenido su contrato fracasado con la RCA en el que habían llegado a hacer una grabación."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 2. Unknown Pleasures

podcast.title: Failed Echo Replication
podcast.body: During the "Heartbreak Hotel" session, RCA engineers attempted but failed to replicate Sam Phillips' distinctive slapback echo sound, resorting to a makeshift echo chamber instead. "The session to record Heartbreak Hotel started with the engineers trying and failing to get a replica of Sam Phillips' slapback echo sound."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 38: "Heartbreak Hotel" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Format War with Columbia
podcast.body: Following RCA's refusal to license Columbia's LP technology, a fierce format war erupted. RCA was determined to push its 7-inch, 45 RPM single, though it did release its classical catalog on LPs, which seemed to signal a wavering in the fight. Millions were spent on advertising the advantages of their stackable records. "That led into a brand new format war... It was Columbia versus RCA, each trying to woo other labels and companies and music consumers to adopt their formats."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 1

podcast.title: Graham Parker's Self-Produced Album
podcast.body: After a dispute with Atlantic Records over production control, Graham Parker signed with RCA Records for his album "The Mona Lisa's Sister." Under this label, he was able to produce the entire album himself with members of The Rumour for less than $60,000, demonstrating his commitment to artistic independence. "left Atlantic records, signed to RCA records, and produced the whole album himself."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Angry Young Men Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Hunky Dory Debut & Back Catalog Reissues
podcast.body: RCA was the label for David Bowie's 'Hunky Dory' album (late 1971), which showed the first real evidence of his commercial potential. Following the breakthrough of 'Ziggy Stardust', RCA capitalized on Bowie's new stardom by reissuing his back catalog, including the 1970 'The Man Who Sold the World' and repackaging the 1969 self-titled LP as 'Space Oddity' (album) with new artwork, driving them onto the charts. "Hunky Dory. Bowie's debut on the RCA label and the first real evidence of his commercial potential."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Initial Dislike of Raw Sound
podcast.body: RCA, The Strokes' US label, initially found the raw, low-fidelity recording of "Is This It" to sound "unprofessional." They only understood the artistic intent and left the band to their methods after hearing the tracks played back on an old boombox, which replicated the intended gritty sound. "This didn't sit well with RCA, The Strokes US label. They thought everything sounded unprofessional."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Strokes

podcast.title: Introduction of the 45 RPM Record
podcast.body: RCA invented and introduced the 45 RPM record in 1949 with a larger, one-and-a-half-inch center hole. Their strategy was to promote a proprietary turntable system where users could stack 45s on a spindle for continuous play, requiring RCA-specific equipment. "This goes back to RCA's introduction of the 45 back in 1949. They were the ones to invent it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 3

podcast.title: Involvement in Format War (Late 1940s)
podcast.body: RCA was a participant in the "format war" of the late 1940s, competing with Columbia Records. RCA championed the 7-inch 45 RPM record, which maintained the standard of one song per side, in opposition to Columbia's long-playing album format. "and RCA's 7-inch 45 RPM record, which stuck with the standard one song per side."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris Part 1: B-Sides and Bonus Tracks

podcast.title: Involvement with Peter and the Wolf
podcast.body: RCA is mentioned as the label that "published" *Peter and the Wolf* in 1969. They reportedly decided to re-edit and release the classical work with David Bowie's 1976 narration. It is suggested that RCA and the Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra were motivated by the commercial potential of Bowie's name, as the orchestra's own records struggled with sales, making Bowie's involvement a valuable promotional asset. "se realmente se publicó en 1969 cuando la RCA creó la escorancia de Bogud y pero que también era la filanmonica de la fila a él lo tenía ahí terminado y dijo y pues mira volvamos a editarlo cuando habló con David Bogud."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Pedro y el lobo de David Bowie

podcast.title: Jesse Belvin's Major Label Signing
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin signed with RCA, a major record label known for artists like Elvis Presley, as part of a strategic career move managed by his wife, Joanne. This signing marked his ambition to achieve mainstream stardom as a smooth ballad singer, a deliberate shift from his earlier doo-wop work into a more sophisticated pop market. "Belvin had signed to a major label, RCA, the same label that Elvis Presley was on, and he was going to make a play for the big time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 47: "Goodnight My Love" by Jesse Belvin

podcast.title: Kickbacks and Parker's Influence
podcast.body: Steve Scholls was compromised by Tom Parker because Parker knew Scholls was taking kickbacks from Hill and Range music publishers. This knowledge allowed Parker to exert control over Scholls and potentially inform RCA management about his activities. "Parker had Scholls in his pocket, because he knew that Scholls was taking kickbacks, and could inform Scholls as buses at RCA."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 33: "Mystery Train", by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Lieber & Stoller Contract
podcast.body: Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller were under contract to RCA to work with white pop stars, including Elvis Presley and Perry Como. This contract, though it produced some hits, was not comfortable for either party and ended after about a year. "They were contracted to RCA to work with white pop stars."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 68: "Yakety Yak" by the Coasters

podcast.title: Little Richard's First Label
podcast.body: RCA Records signed Little Richard after Zenas Sears, a DJ impressed by Richard's talent and connections with the label, helped secure the deal. Richard's first single, "Every Hour," released on RCA, was an imitation of Billy Wright's style and did not achieve any success. "Ceeas had connections with RCA records, and impressed by Richard's talent, he got them to sign him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 34: "Tutti Frutti" by Little Richard

podcast.title: Long-standing Female Producer
podcast.body: For nearly four decades, Ethel Gabriel was the only woman producer at RCA Records, a period spanning from the late 1950s. She produced over 2,500 albums and earned at least 15 gold records during her extensive career with the label, making her a formidable figure in music production. "And for nearly four decades, she was the only woman producer at RCA Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Unsung Heroines

podcast.title: Lou Reed's Solo Contract
podcast.body: Lou Reed signed with RCA to pursue his solo career following the breakup of the Velvet Underground. This occurred during a period when he was experiencing financial hardship, had moved back in with his parents, and was working in his father's accounting firm. "Luric vuelve a firmar por la RCA para seguir su carrera en solitario, sin ningún tipo casi de recursos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Tras los pasos de Lou Reed

podcast.title: Major Label Signing for The Isley Brothers
podcast.body: The Isley Brothers signed with RCA Records, a major label, after failing to achieve a hit with smaller independent labels. They presented one of their records to Hugo and Luigi, who then signed them to the label. "They took one of their records to Hugo and Luigi at RCA Records, and the duo signed them up."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 81: "Shout" by the Isley Brothers

podcast.title: Marketed Janice Martin as "Female Elvis"
podcast.body: RCA Records actively tried to market Janice Martin as their "female Elvis," seeking permission from Elvis and Colonel Parker to promote this comparison. "RCA decided to market her as their female Elvis."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Merger and Disc Technology Innovation
podcast.body: RCA fused with Bernliner's Victor company, forming a powerful entity that became instrumental in the discovery and investment in disc technology improvements. This collaboration led to significant advancements in recording quality and format, maintaining a leadership role in the industry until approximately the mid-1970s. "luego se fusionaría con la RCA, y hasta prácticamente mitad de los 70 serían los grandes descubridores y inversores de las mejoras que teníamos en el disco."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial Formatos que fracasaron: Formatos antiguos

podcast.title: Nashville A-Team Collaboration
podcast.body: RCA utilized the Nashville A-team of session musicians, who recorded with major artists like Elvis and Brenda Lee, and later with Roy Orbison during his brief tenure with the label. "recording for RCA with the same Nashville A team that were recording with Elvis and Brenda Lee."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: One of the Biggest Labels
podcast.body: RCA Records was noted as "one of the biggest labels in the world" at the time of Elvis Presley's signing. "RCA, on the other hand, was one of the biggest labels in the world."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 38: "Heartbreak Hotel" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Pioneer of Vinyl Matrix Gold Records
podcast.body: RCA had a unique practice of awarding gold records in the early days of vinyl. When a record sold so many copies that the vinyl pressing matrix wore out and needed replacement, RCA would take the last unit pressed from the old matrix before switching to new ones. This "gold record" served to commemorate the immense sales that necessitated the matrix change.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Qué es un disco de ORO?    cómo se concede?

podcast.title: Pioneering Stereo and Disco Releases
podcast.body: RCA Records was at the forefront of technical innovation with Ethel Gabriel's involvement in the first stereophonic recordings, including supervising Bing Crosby's first stereo session. The label also embraced new genres, releasing its first disco records with Gabriel's contributions, demonstrating forward-thinking in both technology and genre. "She even supervised the first-ever stereo recording session for Bing Crosby, and she was involved with RCA's first-ever disco releases."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Driven By Her: Unsung Heroines

podcast.title: Poaching of Hugo and Luigi
podcast.body: RCA Records successfully poached producers Hugo and Luigi from Roulette Records after about a year. Morris Levy, the owner of Roulette, allowed them to leave but only if they gave up their shares in Roulette for significantly less than their actual worth. "After a year or so with Roulette, they were in turn poached by RCA."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 81: "Shout" by the Isley Brothers

podcast.title: Proprietary Spindle System
podcast.body: RCA's 45 RPM records, with their large center holes, were designed to be played on RCA record players equipped with a special spindle. This proprietary design aimed to ensure that consumers would purchase RCA's turntables to play their new format. "First of all, if you wanted to play these records, you had to buy an RCA record player with a special spindle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock Explainer 3

podcast.title: Reissue of The Shags' *Philosophy of the World*
podcast.body: RCA Records reissued The Shags' album *Philosophy of the World* in 1999 and has kept it in print ever since. This action reflects the album's legendary status and enduring cult following within outsider music circles, making it widely accessible to new listeners. "The cult of the shags is now so big that RCA records reissued Philosophy of the World in 1999, and have kept it in print ever since."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Outsider Music

podcast.title: Rejection of Jerry Lee Lewis
podcast.body: RCA Records, the label Elvis was on, rejected Jerry Lee Lewis during an audition, telling him he needed to play guitar rather than piano. "He'd already tried RCA records... They told him he needed to play a guitar."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 59: "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On" by Jerry Lee Lewis

podcast.title: Resistance to LP Format (Early 1950s)
podcast.body: In the early 1950s, RCA was difficult about adopting the 12-inch 33 1/3 RPM long-playing album, insisting that their 7-inch 45 RPM single was the future and that consumers did not want song collections. "But our CA was being difficult, insisting that no one really wanted collections of songs and that their 7 inch 45 RPM single was the way the future."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Vinyl: Part 2

podcast.title: Scrapped Album Project
podcast.body: In early 1978, Joy Division attempted to record an album for RCA Records, but the project "didn't work out" and was entirely scrapped before any significant material could be completed or released. "They tried recording an album for RCA Records in early 1978, but that didn't work out, and the whole thing was scrapped before anything significant was accomplished."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Second Largest Record Label
podcast.body: RCA Records was described as the second largest record label in the world at the time The Strokes signed with them after a major bidding war. "la Recia, después se vieron de la segunda escográfica más grande del mundo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: The Strokes: Is this it y su portada censurada.

podcast.title: Stereo Record Pickup Development (Late 1950s)
podcast.body: RCA's radio and controller division developed, designed, and manufactured a special stereo pickup for playing "Living Stereo" records. This pickup utilized two ceramic bars, allowing a single stylus to read the two separate soundtracks etched into the V-shaped groove. "When this pickup, the stylus is passing the two ceramic bars instead of one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of Stereo: Part 2

podcast.title: Steve Scholls' Role
podcast.body: Steve Scholls served as the head of country and R&B at RCA Records and was a key member of Tom Parker's team, handling record production for artists like Eddie Arnold. "Steve Scholls, the head of country and Arvin B at RCA, would handle the record production."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 33: "Mystery Train", by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Struggled to Build Janice Martin's Audience
podcast.body: Despite initial success with Janice Martin's debut single, RCA had trouble building her audience, as they, like many labels in 1956, were unsure how to market white rock and roll acts beyond the absolute biggest stars. "They were having trouble building her audience."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 40: "Drugstore Rock 'n' Roll" by Janis Martin

podcast.title: Vocal Isolation Booth Development
podcast.body: Inspired by Roy Orbison's makeshift coat-rack vocal isolation technique during the "Running Scared" sessions at Monument, Chet Atkins arranged for RCA to build a proper vocal isolation booth at their studios to achieve the same effect. "Apparently, when Chef Hackens popped into the studio for a visit, he was utterly bemused by what he saw, but then he was impressed enough by the idea that he got RCA to build a proper vocal isolation booth at their studios to get the same effect."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: Wu Tang Clan's Debut Contract (No Advance)
podcast.body: The Wu Tang Clan secured a contract with RCA, one of the world's most significant record labels, for their debut album. However, despite the major label backing, RCA did not provide any financial advance ("not a single penny") to produce the record, forcing the band to fund it themselves. This unique contract, championed by RZA, was designed to protect the individual members' rights to pursue solo careers independently of the group's contract. "Al final lo consigo con la RCA y aunque lo firma con una de las esporafilas más importantes en el mundo es como si en la práctica no lo hubiera hecho porque no es dio ni un centimo para hacer el disco."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
